title: Building and Using a Maximum Power Point Tracker for Perovskite Solar Cells
author: Sanz-Marco, Jeronimo-Cruz, et al.
materials: Here, we describe the steps for downloading and installing the software and algorithms needed before assembling the Perovskino.1.Install Arduino IDE software and libraries for the breakouts.a.Go to https://www.arduino.cc/en/software and download the proper version according to the operating system of the computer (Windows/macOS/Linux).b.Once the Arduino IDE is installed, open the Library Manager tab and install the software libraries listed below:i.Install library “Adafruit MCP4725”.ii.Install library “Adafruit INA219”.2.Download the algorithm code of the Perovskino.Note: The Perovskino firmware version used in this protocol and the previous publication was frozen as a first-release version and deposited in the Zenodo repository.a.Download and unzip the file in https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10647187 where you can find all the scripts and files mentioned in this protocol. This release also can be reached in the GitHub repository under this link https://github.com/ej-jp/perovskino/releases/tag/v0.1.Note: This firmware is a work in progress. Well tested improvements will be released as new versions or releases in the GitHub perovskino web page. The user also can test and/or contribute in this main repository but this is not recommended for deployment. If you still prefer to use this more updated repository, please follow the step 2.b below.b.Go to https://github.com/ej-jp/perovskino and download all the fold by ZIP. Or cloning the GitHub repository, by executing the following command in your terminal (if you have installed Git in your computer).> git clonehttps://github.com/ej-jp/perovskino.3.Install Miniconda and libraries.Note: For data acquisition and recording of serial data for further processing, an environment with a modern Python 3 is necessary. We use a minimal subset of Conda called Miniconda to manage this Python environment in the computer.a.Go to https://docs.anaconda.com/free/miniconda/index.html and download the proper version for your computer system (Windows/macOS/Linux).b.Install Miniconda on your computer following the steps recommended in the web page.c.Open the terminal and execute the next command to know if the installation was correct.> conda infoNote: For Microsoft system, open the Anaconda Powershell system (miniconda3) as a Terminal.Note: For MacOS/Linux, open the default terminal system.Note: If the installation was correct, you will get all the information about your Miniconda version.d.Create a specific environment for the dependencies instead of the base environment called perovskino-env.> conda create -n perovskino-env python=3.12.2 pyserial=3.5 pandas=2.2 matplotlib=3.8.4 scipy=1.12.0e.Check that the new environment was created with the next command.Note: If the new environment was correctly created, this command shows “perovskino-env” and its binaries route.> conda env listf.Active the new environment with the next command.Note: The new environment is activated if the line command of the terminal starts with the string (perovskino-env) user@computer:∼$> conda activate perovskino-env

A full tracker or only the Perovskino shield used in this study will be made available on request, but we may require a payment and/or a completed materials transfer agreement if there is potential for commercial application.

steps.title: Install Arduino IDE & libraries
steps.instruction: Download Arduino IDE version 2.3.2 for Windows/macOS/Linux from https://www.arduino.cc/en/software, install it, open the Library Manager and install the libraries “Adafruit MCP4725” and “Adafruit INA219”.

steps.title: Obtain Perovskino firmware
steps.instruction: Download and unzip the Perovskino v0.1 release from Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.10647187 (or from the GitHub release https://github.com/ej-jp/perovskino/releases/tag/v0.1). Optionally clone the repository with git clone https://github.com/ej-jp/perovskino.

steps.title: Install Miniconda & create env
steps.instruction: Download Miniconda for your OS from https://docs.anaconda.com/free/miniconda/index.html, install it, open a terminal and verify the installation with `conda info`. Create a dedicated environment named **perovskino‑env** with the exact command `conda create -n perovskino-env python=3.12.2 pyserial=3.5 pandas=2.2 matplotlib=3.8.4 scipy=1.12.0e`. Confirm creation with `conda env list`, then activate it with `conda activate perovskino-env` (the original text also mentions `conda active perovskino-env`).

steps.title: Assemble Perovskino shield
steps.instruction: Build the Perovskino shield on a perfboard or on the provided PCB (see Figure 1B). Populate it with a 12‑bit DAC breakout (MCP4725), a 12‑bit digital power monitor breakout (INA219), an N‑channel MOSFET (IRLZ34N), a 10 kΩ NTC thermistor (MF52), a 100 nF ceramic capacitor, two 1 kΩ resistors, a 10 kΩ resistor, and two‑pin screw terminals. For the PCB version, follow the Gerber files available in Zenodo or GitHub; if using a 5‑pin Adafruit MCP4725, solder the pad that links VGATE to pin 5. Mount the completed shield on top of an Arduino UNO (Rev3). The assembly time is approximately 2 h.

steps.title: Upload I2C address checker
steps.instruction: Connect the assembled tracker (shield + Arduino UNO) to the computer via USB. Download `i2c_scanner.ino` from https://playground.arduino.cc/Main/sourceblock_1/index.txt?action=sourceblock&num=1, open it in the Arduino IDE, select **Board → Arduino UNO** and the correct COM/Serial port (identify the new port after reconnecting the USB). Compile and upload the sketch, then open the Serial Monitor to read the I2C addresses (e.g., 0x40 for INA219 and 0x60 for MCP4725). If the addresses differ, edit the corresponding constants in the Perovskino `.ino` files. This step takes about 10 min.

steps.title: Upload INA219 calibration firmware (first use)
steps.instruction: After confirming the I2C addresses, open the sketch `INA219-calibration-ino.ino` (included in the downloaded firmware), ensure the parameters `correcV = 0` and `correcI = 1`, compile and upload it to the tracker. This prepares the device for voltage and current calibration.

steps.title: Configure Python data acquisition
steps.instruction: In a terminal, activate the environment (`conda activate perovskino-env`). Identify the tracker’s COM/Serial port: on Windows it appears as **COM#**, on macOS/Linux as **/dev/tty.*** (or **/dev/cu.***). List ports on macOS/Linux with `ls /dev/tty.*`; on Windows use the provided `chgport` utility. Edit the file `perovskino-0.1/codes/02_MPP-algorithms/capture_and_grapher/capture-datos-mpp-temperature.py` lines 7‑9 to set `portpc` to the identified port (comment out any other `portpc` lines with `#`). Run the acquisition with `python capture-datos-mpp-temperature.py`. Data are saved as CSV files in `perovskino-0.1/codes/02_MPP-algorithms/capture_and_grapher/dataraw`. Stop acquisition with **Ctrl+C**. The whole Python‑side preparation is estimated to take 1–3 h.

steps.title: Plot collected data
steps.instruction: For live monitoring, open a new terminal, activate the environment, and run `python grapher4_alive.py`. For post‑run analysis, activate the environment and run `python grapher2.py`. Both scripts read the CSV files in the `dataraw` folder and display voltage, current, power, and temperature. Stop the scripts with **Ctrl+C**. The CSV files can also be opened in any preferred plotting program.

steps.title: Calibrate INA219 voltage & current
steps.instruction: Connect a stable solar cell to the tracker and place a reliable multimeter between the cell and the INA219. **Voltage calibration**: set the MCP4725 DAC to a low value (`countermpp = 1`) to keep the MOSFET off (open‑circuit). Vary the illumination over 5–6 different power levels, record the multimeter voltage and the INA219 voltage shown in the Serial Monitor, and determine `correcV` as the intercept of a linear fit with slope 1. **Current calibration**: set the DAC to a high value (`countermpp = 4095`) to turn the MOSFET fully on (short‑circuit). Again vary illumination over 5–6 levels, record multimeter current and INA219 current, and compute `correcI` as the slope of the linear fit. Upload the updated calibration parameters by re‑uploading the `INA219-calibration-ino.ino` sketch. The INA219 can measure up to **+26 V** and **±3.2 A**; the default calibration line in the code is `ina219.setCalibration_16V_400mA()`. This calibration step takes 1–3 h.

steps.title: Check MOSFET operation
steps.instruction: Illuminate a silicon (or other stable) solar cell with ~1 SUN (≈100 mW cm⁻²). Upload the sketch `mosfet-checker-ino.ino` to the tracker, then run `capture_and_grapher/capture-datos.py` (edit the port if needed) to acquire MOSFET voltage and current data. Generate plots with `capture_and_grapher/grapher2.py` to verify smooth JV curves and absence of glitches. This step ensures the N‑MOSFET functions correctly before MPPT experiments.

steps.title: Run basic JV‑SOP MPPT experiment
steps.instruction: Upload the SOP firmware located in `perovskino-0.1/codes/02_MPP-algorithms/SOP` (edit the `.ino` file to set the desired cycling times for the JV and Stabilized Output Power stages). Connect the solar cell, start data acquisition with `capture-datos-mpp-temperature.py`, and let the tracker continuously alternate JV measurement and SOP stages, thereby tracking the maximum power point (VMPP) in real time. Use the grapher scripts to monitor VMPP, power, and temperature live or after the run.

steps.title: Run P&O MPPT mode (high‑hysteresis cells)
steps.instruction: Upload the Perturb‑and‑Observe (P&O) `.ino` file from the Perovskino v0.1 release (found in the `02_MPP-algorithms` folder). The algorithm first performs a forward (FWD) and a backward (BWD) JV scan to locate two VGATE values that give maximum power; it then sets the current set‑point to the average of these VGATE values and runs the P&O control for the desired duration (e.g., 3 h) under variable illumination (EN‑50530‑type). Acquire data with the same capture script as in step 7 and plot with the grapher scripts. The P&O firmware can be edited to change stage times or algorithm parameters.

description: Researchers investigating emerging solar cell technologies, such as perovskite solar cells (PSCs), often face challenges when conducting extended operational stability assessments due to the limited availability of cost-effective equipment. While determining solar cell efficiency through acquiring a JV curve can be swiftly accomplished within seconds or minutes using a basic potentiostat under controlled illumination, evaluating the operational stability of these devices, particularly by tracking the maximum power point output (MPPT), requires prolonged time-consuming use of costly potentiostat and solar simulator equipments. These equipments are often in high demand for other researching tasks, making it difficult to dedicate them solely to stability assessments. To address this challenge, we have developed a protocol that allows for a preliminary screening of the best performing solar cells without significant economic and space impact in the laboratory. This protocol involves the use of a simple tracker and their operational modes that enable the gathering of statistically significant stability data into a computer (Figure 1A). Our recent work introduced a galvanostatic MPPT algorithm that offers continuous and precise power tracking, enhancing the performance, particularly of challenging high-hysteresis PSCs, which is crucial for propelling PSCs closer to commercial feasibility.Figure 1Solar tracking system components and electrical connections(A) General overview of the system usage consisting of PC, two trackers and two solar cells.(B) Arduino UNO and Perovskino shield (the tracker) device connection scheme.
